    UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                        O R D E R
1. Heard Ms. Iram Majid, learned counsel for the petitioner
and Ms. Garima Jain, learned counsel for the State.
2. The present petition calls in question the correctness of
the judgment/order dated 27-07-2023 in JCRLA No. 88/2009
passed by the High Court of Odisha at Cuttack. By the said
judgment/order, the High Court confirmed the judgment passed

## Page 183

2
by  the  Sessions  Judge,  Mayurbhanj,  Baripada,  Odisha  in
S.T.Case No.204/2007 dated 31.07.2009 which judgment convicted
the petitioner for the offence punishable under Section 302 of
the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and sentenced him to undergo
rigorous imprisonment for life with fine of Rs.1,000/- and in
default thereof, to undergo rigorous imprisonment of one
month. Being aggrieved, the petitioner is before us.
3. When the matter came up on 04.05.2026, this Court made
the following order
“1. Delay condoned.
2. Having heard Ms. Iram Majid, learned counsel for
the petitioner, we are not inclined to interfere with
the impugned order.
3. At this stage, learned counsel for the petitioner
submits that petitioner has undergone 19 years in
custody and that he is entitled to remission.
4. To consider the question of remission, let a copy
of this petition be given to the learned Standing
Counsel for the State of Odisha, returnable on 26th
May, 2026.
5. Learned counsel for the State may take instruction
about the aspect of remission under the applicable
Rules of the State concerned and be ready with the
matter on that aspect on the said date.”
4. As is clear, though we were not inclined to interfere
with the impugned judgment/order, considering the submission
of the learned counsel for the petitioner that the petitioner
has already undergone 19 years in custody as on 04.05.2026, we
wanted from the learned Standing Counsel to take instructions
and  to  report  to  us  about  considering  the  case  of  the

## Page 184

3
petitioner under the applicable Rules for remission.
5. When  the  matter  came  up  on  13.07.2026,  the  learned
Standing Counsel reported that the case of the petitioner will
be considered under the remission Rules.
6. Today, an affidavit has been filed by the State annexing
the proceeding of the special meeting of the State Sentence
Review Board (for short, ‘SSRB’) held on 05.08.2026.
7. All that is mentioned, insofar as the consideration of
the case of the petitioner for remission, is as follows: -
“A detailed discussion was held with regard to the
crime committed by the Life Convict Kalia @ Baula
Singh  and  also  about  the  views  offered  by  the
district  authorities  of  Mayurbhanj.  As  per  the
district authorities of Mayurbhanj, during enquiry it
was ascertained that if the convict to be released on
premature release he may be prejudicial to the public
peace and tranquillity in his locality and may be
absconded after committing any further offence as
learnt reliably during local and confidential enquiry
As  a  result,  the  district  authorities  have  not
recommended his case for premature release.
The Board felt it cogent and unanimously rejected the
case of Life Convict Kalia @ Baula Singh of Circle
Jail, Baripada for premature release from Jail.”
8. Learned counsel for the State submits that detailed
reasons have been set out in the affidavit filed by the State
about  the  justification  for  declining  the  case  of  the
petitioner for remission.
9. We have perused the said affidavit. The affidavit makes a
vague  reference  to  a  confidential  ground-level  inquiry

## Page 185

4
reporting that the convict’s premature release is likely to be
prejudicial to public peace and tranquility.  The very same
affidavit states that for the last 19 years, the convict has
never been released on any kind of leave and also that two of
his three sons have passed away.  It states that socio-economic
reintegration support from the third son, who is a daily labour
with no landed property is inadequate.  There is no reference
to any particular rule in the remission rules which disables
the petitioner from being released on remission.  We find the
reasons set out in the minutes of SSRB dated 05.08.2026 are
wholly unsatisfactory.  There is a reference to the inquiry by
the District Authorities. As to which authority conducted the
inquiry and on what basis the inquiry report concluded against
the release has not been discussed.  None of the relevant
considerations have been adverted to.
10. Under these circumstances, we are left with no option but
to direct that the SSRB to consider the case of the petitioner
for remission afresh under the remission rules after carefully
adverting to all the relevant considerations.
11. Let the needful be done within a period of eight weeks
from today.
12. We set aside the proceedings of the Special Meeting of
the SSRB dated 05.08.2026 and direct the SSRB to consider the
case of the petitioner, de novo.
13. Let a compliance affidavit along with the proceedings of
SSRB be placed before this Court on or before 16.10.2026.

1. We have heard Mr. Arvind Singh Sangwan, learned
Senior counsel for the appellant and Mr. Suryaprakash
V. Raju,  learned Addl. Solicitor General for the
respondent-Union of India.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant  is  aggrieved  by  the  order  dated
30.04.2026 passed by the High Court of Punjab and
Haryana  at  Chandigarh  (briefly  the  ‘High  Court’
hereinafter), rejecting the regular bail application
of the appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  Crime  No.24/2023
registered at NCB, Chandigarh under Sections 8, 18,
29 and 60 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic
1

## Page 188

Substances Act, 1985 (for short, ‘NDPS’).
5. This Court vide order dated 02.06.2026 had issued
notice pursuant to which respondent-Union of India
has filed counter affidavit.
6. Allegation  against  the  appellant  is  of
trafficking  in  opium.  Appellant  was  arrested  on
16.10.2024 on the basis of disclosure statement made
by accused Gulzar Singh.
7. On 03.08.2026, we had passed the following order:
“2. After hearing the matter for some
time, we direct learned counsel for the
respondent-Union of India to inform us on
the next date that out of the remaining
11 prosecution witnesses, who are the
material ones and whether any schedule
has been prepared for hearing of this
case.”
8. Learned counsel for the respondent-Union of India
submits that as of now, 10 witnesses are to be
examined out of which 06 are materials witnesses. He
submits that six months’ time may be granted for
conclusion of the trial.
9. Responding to the above, learned Senior counsel
for the appellant submits that appellant has already
undergone 01 year 10 months of imprisonment. The
three arrested co-accused, i.e. Gulzar Singh, Amarjit
2

## Page 189

Kaur and Jagjit Singh, have been granted bail by the
High Court. It was on the disclosure statement of
accused  Gulzar  Singh  that  appellant  came  to  be
arrested. Now, Gulzar Singh has himself been granted
bail.
10. We feel that binding the Trial Court to a fixed
time schedule for conclusion of the trial may not be
proper  course  in  each  and  every  case.  If  the
appellant makes out a case for bail, bail should be
granted; if not, prayer for bail should be rejected.
11. Insofar  the  present  case  is  concerned,  the
quantity  allegedly  recovered  is  an  intermediate
quantity for which the minimum sentence is 01 year
and the maximum sentence is 10 years.
12. Considering the fact that appellant has already
undergone incarceration for more than 01 year 10
months  and  on  the  principle  of  parity,  we  are
inclined to grant bail to the appellant.
13. Having regard to the above,  the impugned order
dated 30.04.2026 passed by the High Court is set
aside. Consequently, we direct that the appellant
shall be produced before the concerned Special Court
within a maximum period of 07 days from today,
whereafter he shall be released on bail on such terms

and conditions as may be deemed appropriate. We also

2. Leave granted.

1

Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for short, ‘BNS’).
5. This Court vide order dated 03.06.2026 had issued
notice pursuant to which respondent-State of Rajasthan
has filed counter affidavit.
6. Allegation against the appellant is that he is the
head of an institution called Fire & Safety College of
Education which is affiliated to Bharat Sevak Samaj,
Chennai. Entering into a criminal conspiracy with the
other accused persons, appellant had forged the diploma
certificates etc. of certain candidates to make them
eligible for recruitment in the Indian Navy.
7. Learned Senior counsel for the appellant submits
that appellant was arrested in connection with the
related FIR on 21.08.2025 and has been in custody since
then. He has drawn the attention of the Court to the
charge sheet and strenuously argues that no culpability
can be fastened on to the appellant on the basis of
allegations  and  materials  contained  in  the  charge
sheet. He also submits that though charge sheet has
been  filed,  the  trial  has  yet  not  commenced.

CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S).         OF 2026
 (Arising from SLP (Crl.) No(s).  12593/2026)
BADRI    ... APPELLANT(S)
Versus
STATE OF RAJASTHAN ... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal arises from an order dated 17-04-
2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature for
Rajasthan at Jaipur, rejecting the application
of the appellant seeking suspension of sentence
awarded by the trial court during pendency of his
appeal before the High Court. 
4. The submissions on behalf of the appellant is
that as many as fifteen accused were implicated
and only six have been convicted. The appellant
1

## Page 203

has  been  implicated  by  attributing  role  of
carrying a stick in an unlawful assembly. The
serious injury is referrable to an axe which is
attributed to co-accused Ramjivan.
5. In such circumstances, it has been submitted
that the appellant who is now aged 76 years, is
entitled to be released on bail after suspension
of sentence pending consideration of his appeal.
6. The learned Counsel for the State-respondent
has opposed the prayer for bail by submitting that
it is a case where Section 149 IPC has been
invoked.
7. Be that as it may, having regard to the
nature  of  the  allegations  qua  the  appellant,
considering the age of the appellant, we are of
the  view  that  the  appellant  is  entitled  for
suspension of sentence pending consideration of
his appeal by the High Court. 
8. Consequently,  the  appeal  is  allowed.  The
order passed by the High Court rejecting the
prayer for suspension of sentence of the appellant
is set aside.
2

## Page 204

9. The appellant shall be released on bail on
such terms and conditions as the trial court may
deem fit to impose in the facts and circumstances
of the case and the sentence awarded by the trial
court shall remain suspended pending consideration
of the appeal of the appellant.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

4. In this case, it appears that Vinay was an
injured witness. His statement was not recorded at
the  time  when  the  petition  was  filed  and
therefore, hearing on this  petition was deferred
to enable the Trial Court to record the statement
of Vinay.
5. We have been informed that the statement of
Vinay has been recorded in the trial and he has
not  identified  the  appellant  as  one  of  the
participants in the incident.
6. Having  regard  to  the  above,  without
expressing any opinion  on the merits of the case,
the appeal deserves to be allowed.
7. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The order
passed by the High Court rejecting the  bail
prayer of the appellant is set aside.

terms and conditions as the trial court may deem
fit to impose in the facts and circumstances of
the case.

1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. An FIR No. 422/2025 came to be registered against
the appellant on 15.05.2025 at Police Station Seemapuri,
Shahdara, Delhi under Section for the offences punishable
under Sections 309(6), 311, 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023 (“for short BNS”) and appellant is seeking for
being enlarged on regular bail. 
4. The case of the prosecution is that the complainant
came to Delhi on 14.05.2025 in search of employment and
at about 2:30 a.m. he hired an auto rickshaw to go to
(SLP (Crl) No. 14325/2026)                                1

## Page 223

Karnal By pass and at about 2:40 a.m. near underpass at
Vivek Vihar which leads to Seemapuri, the auto driver and
two unknown persons robbed him of Rs. 1,000/- and his
mobile phone and on resisting the same they had assaulted
him with sharp object causing injury to his left hand.
Appellant is in custody since one year three months.
5. On investigation being completed, chargesheet has
been filed and the allegation against the appellant is that
he was one of the unknown persons who had robbed the
complainant. The other co-accused namely Shaukat Ali @
Saukat Ali has been granted bail by the learned trial judge.
After taking note of the contentions raised by the learned
counsel appearing for the parties. 
6. Even before this Court the learned counsel appearing
for the State while opposing the prayer has contended that
the other co-accused is still absconding and there is
likelihood  of  appellant  indulging  in  threatening  the
witnesses or committing similar offences.
7. Having regard to the fact that the co-accused against
whom the same allegation as made against the appellant
(SLP (Crl) No. 14325/2026)                                2

## Page 224

has already been enlarged on bail on the ground of parity,
appellant is entitled to the relief sought for..
8. Hence, we allow this appeal, set aside the impugned
order and direct the appellant to be released on regular bail
on such terms and conditions as the jurisdictional Court
deems fit to impose.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stands consigned
to records.

O R D E R
    1.  Leave granted.
2.  The present appeal has been filed seeking grant of
bail  to  the  appellant  in  FIR  No.0379/2023  dated
20.07.2023  registered  at  Police  Station  Murlipura,
Jaipur (West), under Sections 420, 467, 468, 471, 120-B
and 201 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
3.   The allegation against the appellant is that he
was  involved  in  land  grabbing  cases  using  forged
documents and the appellant was also part of that
larger conspiracy.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant has argued
before this Court that the appellant has been falsely
implicated in this case and he has no role to play in
the crime. The appellant is in jail for the last 13
months. On the other hand, learned counsel appearing on
Criminal Appeal No.    of   2026 @  Special Leave to Appeal (Criminal)  No.10327/2026

## Page 228

2
behalf  of  the  respondent-State  of  Rajasthan  has
vehemently opposed the prayer for grant of bail, on the
ground that the appellant was involved in land grabbing
cases using forged documents and, therefore, he should
not be enlarged on bail. 
5. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and
material placed on record and the fact that he is in
custody  for  the  last  13  months,  we  are  of  the
considered view that the appellant has made out a case
for interference with the impugned judgment and order
dated 16.04.2026.
6. Considering the totality of the circumstances and
the fact that the appellant has been in custody for the
last 13 months, this Court is of the view that his
further detention is not necessary pending trial and,
therefore, we allow the appeal and grant relief as
prayed for by admitting the appellant to an order of
grant of bail. 
7. Appellant shall be released on bail, subject to
furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of the
trial  court  and  subject  to  such  other  terms  and
conditions as may be imposed by it. 
8. Needless to observe, the appellant shall not,
directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat or
promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the facts
of the case from disclosing such facts to the court.
Criminal Appeal No.    of   2026 @  Special Leave to Appeal (Criminal)  No.10327/2026

## Page 229

3
9. In the event there is any breach of the terms and
conditions for grant of bail, the trial court shall be
at liberty to cancel the bail of the appellant.
10.  It  is  also  ordered  that  the  appellant  shall
diligently attend proceedings of the trial, unless
exempted. If he is found to abstain from attending the
proceedings without justifiable cause, that could also
be seen as breach of the conditions for grant of bail
and the trial court will be free to pass appropriate
orders.
11. We clarify that the observations made in this order
and grant of bail will not be treated as findings on
the merits of the case.
12.  The  appeal  is,  accordingly,  allowed  on  the
aforesaid  terms,  and  the  impugned  order  dated
16.04.2026 is set aside. 
13.  Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

## Page 250

2
                             O R D E R
1. Heard Mr. Amit Anand Tiwari, learned Senior Counsel for
the petitioner(s) and Mr. Nikhil Goel, learned Senior Counsel
for the respondent(s).
2. The present petitions call in question the correctness of
the orders dated 08-04-2026 in FMA No. 1601/2025 & 11-05-2026
in RVW No. 125/2026 passed by a Division Bench of the High
Court at Calcutta. 
3. Considering the nature of the order that we propose to
make, only a brief reference to the facts is necessary.
Pursuant to a Notice Inviting Tender (NIT), the petitioner
no.1 had issued a work order dated 11.01.2013 valued at
Rs.3.51 crores approximately for certain constructions with
stipulated deadlines for completing the projects. The exact
contract value was to depend on the quantities of work
executed and measured, subject to certain conditions. Disputes
arose between the parties with regard to the timelines for
completion of the work. Ultimately, the respondent(s) herein
filed a writ petition in WPA No.23506/2017 before the High
Court at Calcutta seeking release of payments under the final
bill as well as the security deposits.
4. The petitioners opposed the said writ petition including
on the ground of maintainability. The learned Single Judge of
the High Court by judgment dated 06.05.2025 dismissed the said
writ petition as it involved disputed questions of facts. The
respondent carried the matter in appeal before the Division

## Page 251

3
Bench of the High Court. By the order of 08.04.2026, the
Division Bench made an interim order directing the petitioners
herein to pay a sum of Rs.90,00,000/- to the respondent. By
the said order while the petitioners were not allowed to
retain the earnest money, security deposit and 10% liquidated
damages. A review petition filed by the petitioners, was
dismissed on 11.05.2026. Being aggrieved, the petitioners
approached this Court.
5. When the matter came up before us on 15.05.2026, while
issuing notice to the respondents, we stayed the impugned
orders.
6. Parties  were  also  referred  to  mediation  to  find  an
amicable solution of the disputes.
7. Today, both the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
in respective parties jointly report that the mediation has
failed.
8. However, both parties made a prayer to this Court that
they are agreeable to have the disputes inter se arising in
this matter between the parties to be resolved under the
Arbitration & Conciliation Act, 1996(for short, ‘A&C Act’). 
9. The consent of both the parties to refer the matter to an
arbitrator is placed on record. 
10. Parties have also left it to the Court to appoint an
arbitrator. 
11. Considering the nature of the dispute involved between
the parties, we appoint Mr.Rishav Banerjee(+919051330097),
Advocate practicing in the Kolkata, to act as an arbitrator in

## Page 252

4
this matter. 
12. Parties to get in touch with the learned Arbitrator. The
fees shall be in accordance with Fourth Schedule of the A&C
Act. 
13. In view of the agreement arrived at between the parties
to refer the matter to arbitration, the interim order granted
by this Cout on 15.05.2026 shall continue till the learned
Arbitrator  is  moved  for  a  suitable  modification.  The
arbitrator shall decide the interim application, if any,
moved, uninfluenced by any of the observations made in the
orders of the High Court or by the order of this Court.
14. In view of this order, nothing further remains to be
adjudicated in FMA No.1601/2025 and the same will stand
disposed of. 
15. All contentions of the parties are left open.  
16. The Special Leave Petitions are disposed of in the above
terms. 
17. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

CIVIL APPEAL No.4852/2024
DABUR INDIA LIMITED   APPELLANT
VERSUS
NATIONAL BIODIVERSITY AUTHORITY           RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Challenge in this appeal under Section 22 of the National Green Tribunal
Act, 20101 is to a judgment and order dated 20 th December, 20232 passed by
the National Green Tribunal, Southern Zone at Chennai 3 on Appeal No.54 of
2022.
2. The Tribunal, after examining the order under challenge 4 before it passed
by the National Biodiversity Authority5 on its own merits, found the same to be
lacking in reasons; hence, the Tribunal set aside the impugned order and
ordered a remand. The NBA was directed to reconsider its earlier order and in
doing so, to follow the principles of natural justice.  The appeal, thus, stood
allowed on the aforesaid terms.
3. The impugned order of the tribunal was not stayed by this Court while
notice was issued on this appeal; however, noting that an order on remand
1  NGT Act, 20102  impugned order3  Tribunal4  dated 04th August, 2022 5  NBA
1

## Page 270

could have been passed in terms of the impugned order, liberty was granted to
the appellant to place it on record.
4. It is not in dispute that in terms of the impugned order of the Tribunal the
NBA has passed a fresh order6 rejecting the claim of the appellant.
5. Mr. V Lakshmikumaran, learned senior counsel for the appellant, seeks to
assail the impugned order on the various grounds urged by him. However, an
objection has been raised on behalf of the respondents.  According to learned
counsel representing them, the fresh order passed by the NBA, on remand, is
amenable to a challenge before the Tribunal under Section 16(j) of the NGT Act,
2010 and, therefore, the appellant ought to be relegated to such remedy.
6. Mr. V Lakshmikumaran does not dispute that an appeal is available;
however, he submits that if indeed this Court were inclined to grant liberty to
the appellant to challenge the order afresh before the Tribunal, the impugned
order of the NGT, to the extent it contains observations affecting the interest of
the appellant, may be set aside.
7. Having heard learned counsel for the parties, we dispose of this appeal
granting liberty to the appellant to challenge the order of the NBA dated 18 th
April, 2024, passed on remand, in a fresh appeal under Section 16(j) of the NGT
Act.
8. Should an appeal be instituted within 30 (thirty) days from this date, the
Tribunal will proceed to decide the appeal on merits and limitation, in such
case, will not stand as a bar.
9. We also observe that since we are refraining from examining the
impugned order on its own merits, having regard to a subsequent order of
rejection having surfaced, the Tribunal while proceeding to decide the appeal, if
6  dated 18th April, 2024 
2

## Page 271

filed, shall do so without being influenced by any observation made in the
impugned order.
10. All points and contentions on merits are kept open.
11. The civil appeal is disposed of on the aforesaid terms.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

1. Read the office report dated 11th August, 2026.
2. Despite service of notice of this transfer petition under Section
25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 presented by Neetu Chauhan
(hereafter the petitioner) on Gautam (hereafter the respondent), he
has not entered appearance.
3. The marriage between the petitioner and the respondent was
solemnized on 17 th February, 2024 according to Hindu rites and
customs. No child was born to the petitioner and the respondent from
the wedlock. However, the parties have since drifted apart owing to
differences arising by and between them.
4. The respondent has instituted proceedings under Section 13 of
the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, bearing Original Case No.2793 of 2025
titled “ Gautam  Vs.  Neetu  Chauhan ” which is pending before the
Principal Judge, Family Court, Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh.
5. On the multiple grounds urged in the petition, the petitioner
1

the Principal Judge, Family Court, Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh  to the
court of the District Judge, Family Court, Gurugram, Haryana.
6. Since  the  respondent  has  not  controverted  the
statements/averments made in the petition, we are of the view that
he has no serious objection to grant of the prayer for transfer.
7. We  are  also  otherwise  satisfied,  having  regard  to  the
inconvenience the petitioner is likely to face if the proceedings were
continued in the Family Court at Ghaziabad , Uttar Pradesh  that
interest of justice demands grant of the prayer for transfer. 
8. Hence, the transfer petition is allowed. Original Case No.2793
of 2025 titled “ Gautam  Vs.  Neetu  Chauhan ” pending before the
Principal Judge, Family Court, Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh is transferred
to the District Judge, Family Court, Gurugram, Haryana . Records of
Original Case No.2793 of 2025 be transferred to the transferee court
immediately.
9. To avoid delay, the parties are directed to appear before the
transferee court on 17 th September, 2026. If any or both the parties
fail to appear on that day, the presiding officer of the transferee court
will fix another date of appearance. Thereafter, he shall be free to
proceed in accordance with law. 
10. The  presiding  officer  shall  endeavour  to  bring  about  a
settlement between the parties through the process of mediation. If
the process is unsuccessful, nothing shall preclude the presiding
officer to take the proceedings to its logical conclusion on its merits
and in accordance with law.

1. Delay condoned.
2. The petitioner before us was put to trial in the Court
of  the  Additional  Sessions  Judge,  Sausar,  District
Chhindwara in Sessions Trial No.05/2022 for the offence of
murder, punishable under Section 302 of the Indian Penal
1

## Page 306

Code, 1860 (for short, “the IPC”).
3. At the end of the trial, the petitioner was held
guilty of the alleged crime and was sentenced to undergo
imprisonment for life with fine of Rs.6,000/-.
4. The petitioner went in appeal before the High Court.
His Criminal Appeal No.9510/2024 was admitted. In the said
appeal,  he  moved  an  I.A.  seeking  suspension  of  the
substantive order of sentence of life imprisonment passed
by the Trial Court and release on bail, pending the final
disposal of his Criminal Appeal.
5. The High Court, instead of deciding the application
seeking suspension of sentence decided to take up the
appeal itself for final hearing.
6. By a very short order, without discussing the evidence
on record, the High Court thought fit to bring the case
within Exception 4 of Section 300 of the IPC and modified
the conviction from Section 302 to Section 304 Part-II of
the IPC.
7. The first fundamental error in the impugned judgment
is that having invoked one of the Exceptions to Section 300
of the IPC, i.e., Exception 4, how can the High Court
convict the accused for Section 304 Part-II of the IPC.
8. Secondly, we also take notice of the fact that the
deceased made oral dying declarations before PW-1 and PW-7,
respectively. There is not discussion in this regard also
in the order.
9. Since this is a legal aid matter, we want to hear the
2

State on all relevant aspects of the matter highlighted
above.
10. Issue notice, returnable on 24.09.2026.
11. Notice  be  also  served  on  the  petitioner-convict
through the Superintendent of the Jail.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. All the special leave petitions have been presented before this Court more
than a year after expiry of the prescribed period of limitation.
2. Cause shown for condonation of delay is not only insufficient, the
petitioner has attempted to hoodwink the Court by taking shelter of falsehood.
3. The applications seeking condonation of delay in presentation of the
special leave petitions stand rejected.
4. Consequently, the special leave petitions are dismissed as time-barred
with  cost of Rs.25,000/- [Rupees twenty-five thousand] only in each such
petition.
5. Let the costs be deposited with the Secretary General of this Court within
two months from date. Once deposited, the Secretary General shall identify four
organizations across the country which are running homes for intellectually
disabled children (children with special needs). Once identified, the amount on
account of costs, as imposed, shall be divided in equal shares and paid to them.
6. Pending interlocutory application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

years rigorous imprisonment, with a fine of Rs.20,000/-
for the offences punishable under Sections 354, 354B,

two years in custody. Learned counsel for the petitioner-
State submits that according to the prosecution it was a
case of an attempt to commit penetrative assault under

the petitioner-State submits that the High Court has
erred on two counts in the impugned order. One is that
the High Court was wrong in recording that the respondent
no.1 was the uncle of the victim and second is that the
High Court erred in observing that prima facie it appears
to be a case of Section 7 of the POCSO Act. 
3. Notwithstanding these, we are not inclined to interfere
with the impugned order in exercise of our jurisdiction
under Article 136 of the Constitution of India.
4. Needless to observe that these observations are only for
the purpose of considering the application for suspension
of sentence of respondent no.1 and the appeal be heard on
its own merits before the High Court.

terms.

2. Leave granted.
3. Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  has  placed
before us Standing Order No. 826(E) of the Government
of  India  as  published  in  the  Gazette  of  India:
Extraordinary,  declaring  narcotics  substances  and
preparations mentioned to be manufactured drugs. Serial
No.(35) is relevant and it reads thus:
“(35) Methyl morphine (commonly known as
‘Codeine’) and Ethyl morphine and their
salts (including Dionine), all dilutions
and preparations, except those which are
compounded  with  one  or  more  other
ingredients and containing not more than
100 milligrams of the drug per dosage unit
and with a concentration of not more than
35 per cent in undivided preparations and
which have been established in therapeutic
practice.”
4. On the aforesaid basis, learned counsel for the
appellant  argues  that  the  contraband  allegedly
recovered from the appellant falls in the category of
manufactured drugs.
5. Learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of
Himachal Pradesh has referred to paragraph No.55 of the
judgment and conviction of the Trial Court to submit
that the substance mentioned by the appellant and the
substance recovered from his possession are different.
What was recovered from the appellant was ‘Codeine
Phosphate’ whereas Clause-35 of the Standing Government
2

## Page 340

order refers to ‘Methyl Morphine’, which is commonly
known as ‘Codeine’.
6. Be that as it may, having regard to the fact that
appellant has already undergone more than 04 years of
incarceration and an arguable case has been made out,
we are inclined to suspend the sentence and grant bail
to the appellant.
7. Consequently, we direct that the appellant shall
be produced before the concerned Special Court within a
maximum period of 07 days from today, whereafter he
shall be released on bail on such terms and conditions
as may be deemed appropriate.
8. Hearing of the appeal be expedited.

       IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal No.12054/2016
THE STATE OF ARUNACHAL PRADESH    APPELLANT
VERSUS
SHRI DIMBESWAR PAWE      RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. The  present  appeal  is  directed  against  the  judgment  and
order1 dated 06th October, 2015 passed by the High Court of Gauhati.
2. By the impugned judgment, the order of dismissal from service
imposed on the respondent by the appellant-State was converted to
compulsory  retirement.  The  High  Court  having  found  that  the
respondent had crossed the age of superannuation, it was held that
he would only be entitled to superannuation benefits.
3. Mr.  Rauf  Rahim,  learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant, has contended that the High Court went out of its way and
generously substituted the penalty imposed upon the respondent.
According to him, the respondent was not entitled to any relief, much
less the relief granted, having regard to his conduct of being involved
in embezzlement in excess of Rs.5,00,000/- (Rupees five lakh) only.
4. We have considered the submission made by Mr. Rahim with
the attention and seriousness the same deserves.
5. However, we are of the opinion that the respondent having
retired from service even during the pendency of the proceedings
1  impugned judgment
1

## Page 351

before the High Court and a decade having passed since then, it
would be imprudent, in the special facts and circumstances noted by
the High Court, to take back the superannuation benefits to which he
has been held entitled.
6. Therefore, keeping the question of law open, the appeal stands
dismissed.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

(DIPANKAR DATTA)
………………………………………….J
(SHEEL NAGU)

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Respondent was dismissed from service on 25 th June, 2007 following
disciplinary proceedings. He challenged the order of dismissal before the
Maharashtra Administrative Tribunal 1. The Tribunal set aside the order of
dismissal; but, based on proof of charges 1, 2, 8 and 10, it required the
disciplinary authority to revisit the question of penalty.
2. The State of Maharashtra challenged the order of the Tribunal before the
Division Bench of the High Court of Bombay which refused to interfere
1  Tribunal
1

## Page 354

therewith. 
3. Upon the order of dismissal of the writ petition by the High Court being
carried before this Court, a coordinate Bench while issuing notice on 10 th
October, 2017 stayed the operation of the order of the Tribunal. 
4. We are informed that the respondent has since passed away on 19 th June,
2026.
5. Had he remained in service, the respondent would in any case have
superannuated on 30th June, 2016.
6. Since the respondent is no longer alive, question of imposition of an order
of penalty on him does not arise.
7. It is noted that by an order dated 16th November, 2022 passed by another
coordinate Bench of this Court, the State of Maharashtra was directed to place
its stand having regard to the passage of time and looking to the nature of the
order passed by the Tribunal.
8. Since appropriate instructions were not made available to learned
counsel, the special leave petition remained pending. Ultimately, special leave
to appeal was granted on 20th May, 2024.
9. We require Mr.  Aaditya Aniruddha Pande, learned counsel appearing for
the State of Maharashtra, to place before us a calculation of the emoluments
that the deceased respondent would have earned between the period 25 th June,
2007 and 30 th June, 2016, had he not been dismissed, and also during the
period 01st July, 2016 to 19th June, 2026, if were paid his retiral benefits.
10. Once such calculation is placed before us, we propose to consider the
appeal once again and make appropriate orders.
11. Relist the appeal after three weeks.
2

12. In the meanwhile, let steps be taken for bringing on record the heirs/legal

IA No. 233128/2026 - STAY APPLICATION
 
Date : 12-08-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE THE CHIEF JUSTICE
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE JOYMALYA BAGCHI
         HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE V. MOHANA
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Ashok K. Mahajan, AOR
                   Mr. Dr. Surat Singh, Adv.
                   Mr. Adarsh Tevatia, Adv.
                                      
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The Centre for Law and Good Governance, a non-political
public-spirited academic organization, has approached this Court
under Article 32 of the Constitution of India through the instant
writ  petition,  purportedly  filed  in  public  interest,  seeking
direction to the Union of India, State Governments, and Union
Territories to formulate a uniform policy regarding regularization
and demolition of long-standing unauthorized constructions. For
that purpose, the petitioner also seeks appointment of an Expert
Committee by this Court to monitor and supervise the formulation
and implementation of such policies.
2. It is, inter alia , pointed out that State Governments across
1

## Page 360

the country have, for decades, not only allowed unauthorized
colonies and constructions to stand unchallenged, but they have
also been facilitating implied regularisation of such development
by assessing municipal taxes, sanctioning electricity and water
connections, and converting leasehold properties into freehold.
Such like policies are said to be in vogue in the States of Andhra
Pradesh and Telangana and the NCT of Delhi. However, there are
other States where the unauthorized colonies constructed decades
back are suddenly ordered to be demolished, with or without notice,
but without any welfare scheme for rehabilitation of the affected
families. It is in this backdrop that the petitioner contends that
demolition, being an extreme and irreversible measure, cannot be
carried  out  without  a  policy  that  reconciles  enforcement  of
planning laws with the rights to shelter, livelihood, and dignity
as guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution.
3. The petitioner, thus, prays for this Court to issue various
directions, as briefly pointed out at the outset of this order.
4. We  have  heard  learned  counsel  for  the  petitioner  at  a
considerable length. 
5. While we appreciate the concern of the petitioner–organisation
regarding rehabilitation of the persons, whose right to shelter is
adversely impacted as a result of demolition, etc., we are also of
the view that such issues essentially fall within the State’s
domain of policy. The factual circumstances vary from State to
State and would, therefore, warrant variation in their policy
decision as well. It may not be prudent for this Court to lay down
2

## Page 361

any uniform policy framework to be applied in all the States.
6. That being so, we deem it appropriate to dispose of this
petition with liberty to the petitioner to forward a copy of its
writ petition to Union of India, the respective State Governments,
and the Union Territories, for a competent authority to consider
the issues raised therein for the purpose of formulation or
revisiting their existing policies.
7. We are hopeful that due consideration shall be given to all
such issues by such authority.
8. The Writ Petition, thus, stands disposed of in the above
terms.
9. All pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
(ARJUN BISHT)                              (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        DY. REGISTRAR

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.            OF 2026
(@SLP(CRL.) NO.10355 of 2026)
MOHAMMED YASIR ALIAS YASIR ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF KERALA  ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. The appellant has been arraigned as an accused in FIR No.1297/2025
which is registered for the offences punishable under Sections 126,
118(1) and 110 read with Section 3(5) of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
(BNS). In all six persons have been arraigned as accused,  Firos  was
arraigned as Accused No.2 while appellant herein as Accused No.1.
4.  Accused no.2-Firos sought for grant of regular bail and it has been
held in the order dated 13.01.2026 that the investigation was almost
over and injury sustained are not so serious whereas the same Judge in
the impugned order dated 31.03.2026 opines that the complainant has
sustained serious injury and the investigation is at preliminary stage.
The allegations made against the appellant and Firos are one and the
same. As Firos has been released on bail, the appellant is also entitled
to be released on bail on the ground of parity. However, learned counsel
appearing for the respondent-State has vehemently opposed granting
1                                                                              SLP(CRL.) NO.10355 of 2026 

## Page 375

of bail on the ground that Firos was granted regular bail and appellant is
seeking anticipatory bail.
5. The fact remains that there cannot be any change in the nature of
injury sustained by the complainant, that apart, there is a cross-FIR
namely FIR No.1302/2025 filed in which Firos is the complainant. Having
regard to the totality of the circumstances, namely, there being cross-
FIR and co-accused having already been granted bail, we are of the
considered view that appellant is entitled for grant of anticipatory bail
and undisputedly after the interim protection was granted by this Court
vide order dated 10.06.2026, the appellant has been appearing before
the Investigating Officer (IO) and cooperating with the investigation.
Hence, his custodial interrogation is not warranted.
6.  For the commutative reasons aforestated, we allow this appeal and
set aside the impugned order. Appellant is ordered to be released on
anticipatory bail on such terms and conditions as the jurisdictional IO
may deem fit to impose. 
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

applications by the High Court in connection with FIR No. 110 of
2026 dated 14.04.2026 registered with Police Station Ganj, Raipur,
for the offence punishable under Section 7 of the Chhattisgarh
Gambling (Prohibition) Act, 2022.
3. Charge-sheet No.102 of 2026 was filed on 10.06.2026, including
S.112(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,2023. The petitioners were,
named in the charge-sheet as Accused No.22/Rohit Singh, arrested on
17.04.2026; Accused No.6/Shubham Sithlani, arrested on 15.04.2026;
Accused No.11/Tulsidas Namdev @ Prince, Arrested on 17.04.2026; and
Accused No.28/Sandeep Israni, arrested on 01.05.2026.
4. The petitioners are accused of being involved in an organized
online gambling group, which runs online cricket betting through an
app  called  “3  Stumps”,  based  on  disclosure  statements  of
co-accused.
5. The impugned Orders have been challenged by raising grounds
such as the petitioners are not named in the FIR; that implication
is based on alleged disclosure statements; that investigation is
admittedly complete; and the delay in trial, since 38 witnesses are
to be examined.

judgment and order of conviction passed by the Trial Court

authority of the State Government seeking remission of
sentence, after undergoing sentence for a further period of
one year.
4. If  any  such  representation  is  preferred  by  the
petitioner-convict, the State shall look into the same at
the  earliest  and  take  an  appropriate  decision ,  in
accordance with the remission policy prevailing at the
time of the commission of the alleged offence, or any
other  policy  that  may  be  more  beneficial  to  the
petitioner.

disposed of.

O R D E R
1.  The Petitioner seeks transfer of the industrial dispute case
filed by him before the Presiding Officer, Labour Court/ Industrial
Court,  Haldwani,  Uttarakhand  to  the  Presiding  Officer,  Labour
Court/Industrial Court, Reasi, Jammu & Kashmir.
2. The petitioner has contended that since he is a poor labourer
and residing in Reasi, Jammu & Kashmir, the proceedings should be
transferred there.
3. We are of the opinion that simply because the petitioner is
residing  in  Reasi,  that  cannot  be  a  ground  to  transfer  the
proceedings from the Industrial Court, Haldwani, Uttarakhand to the
Industrial Court, Reasi, Jammu & Kashmir. 
4. However, the petitioner would be at liberty to seek hearing by
virtual mode, if such facility is available in the Court of Reasi,
Jammu & Kashmir or to be represented by a counsel, as may be
desirable.
5. The Transfer Petition is dismissed with the above observations.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
…………………………………………………………………. J.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following

1. Delay condoned.
2. Heard  Mr.  Nitin  Gaur,  learned  counsel  for  the
petitioners. Learned counsel drawing attention to page 60 (pdf
82) of the paper books submits that the denial of interest by
this Court in the main round of litigation between the parties
in paragraph 10 appears to be an inadvertent error. Learned
counsel submits that the Reference Court at Shahdol (page 40,
pdf 62) which granted Rs.4.46 per square foot, further granted
30%  solatium  and  also  ordered  interest.  Learned  counsel

## Page 516

2
submits that the High Court (page 56, pdf 78) though reduced
the square foot price to Rs.3/-, expressly directed that
interest on solatium had to be paid in paragraph 21. In this
background the only question before this Court in the earlier
round was whether the High Court was justified in reducing the
per square foot price/compensation. Learned counsel relies on
the Constitution Bench Judgment of this Court in “Sunder vs.
Union  of  India”  reported  in  (2001)  7  SCC  211,  more
particularly, in paragraph  27 thereof.
3. We have prima facie  of the opinion that the petitioners
is right.
4. However,  considering  the  order  of  this  Court  dated
14.05.2015 is of three Hon’ble Judges, we are of the opinion
that the matter be placed before Hon’ble the Chief Justice of
India to constitution of an appropriate Bench.

For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The Division Bench of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay 1 by the
impugned order dated 07th August, 2026 has directed possession of the secured
asset to be made over to the secured creditor – Punjab National Bank – on 17 th
August, 2026, in pursuance of the order under Section 14 of the Securitisation
and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act,
20022.
2. Grievance of the petitioners – borrowers – is that the said order under
1 High Court
2 SARFAESI Act
1

## Page 596

Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act is the subject-matter of challenge in a pending
application under Section 17 thereof before the Debts Recovery Tribunal3.
3. According to Mr. S. Niranjan Reddy, learned senior counsel, the secured
creditor, without waiting for the order to be passed on the application under
Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act, has obtained an order which operates to the
serious detriment and prejudice of the petitioners. 
4. We find no stay having been granted by the DRT on the application under
Section 17 of the SARFAESI Act.
5. In such view of the matter, there was no bar for the secured creditor to
move the High Court for obtaining an order for police assistance to be accorded
to implement the order under Section 14 of the SARFAESI Act.
6. We see no reason to interfere with the impugned judgment and order of
the High Court; hence, the special leave petition stands dismissed.
7. However, we make it clear that the application under Section 17 of the
SARFAESI Act before the DRT shall be decided on its own merits and without
being influenced by reason of possession having been taken over in terms of
the High Court’s order, if at all.
8. Pending applications, if any, shall stand disposed of.

For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Permission to file Special Leave Petition is granted.
2. We have heard Ms. Meenakshi Arora, learned senior counsel and
perused the record.
3. The Special Leave Petition is directed against the impugned
order dated 17.04.2026 passed by the High Court in Writ Petition
(Lodging) No. 12465 of 2026.

## Page 618

2
4. The foremost objection canvassed by the learned senior counsel
is that the impugned judgment has committed an irregularity by
deciding whether the petitioner is a proper and necessary party to
the challenge in Writ Petition (Lodging) No. 12465 of 2026. The
need for the presence of a party is determined on case to case
basis, and the oral prayer is not acceptable to the High Court. The
interest of the petitioner ought not to have been adversely
affected.
5. We have perused the observation made in Para ‘2’ of the
impugned judgment, and we are of the view that shutting out the
petitioner with this observation will have an effect in future or
any litigation regarding the subject matter of the litigation.
6. Therefore, to  the  limited  extent  of  considering  the
correctness of the view taken in Paragraph No. ‘2’, we dispose of
the Special Leave Petition as follows:- 
The  observations  in  Paragraph  No.  ‘2’  of  the
impugned judgment  will not  come in  the way  of  the
petitioner  in  filing  an appropriate  application  for
getting impleaded as one of the respondents in respect of
the present lis/subject matter before the authority or in
the subsequent litigation before the High Court , and it
will be examined on its own merits.
7. The Special Leave Petition stands disposed of with the above
observation.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The issue that has been raised in larger public interest
concerns the removal of blockades on National Highway No. 2 and
restoration of the supply of essential commodities in Kangpokpi
District, Manipur.
2. During the course of hearing, Shri Anand Grover, learned
Senior Counsel representing the Petitioner, points out that there
are a few other National Highways that have also, reportedly, been
blocked in the State of Manipur, and the petitioner–organization,
1

## Page 704

in coordination with other social organizations, seeks restoration
of the functionality of all such National Highways. 
3. The  International  Meitei  Organization  has  also  filed  an
application (I.A. No.243484/2026) for its impleadment in these
proceedings. 
4. On oral mentioning, we take that application on record. The
same is allowed and the applicant–International Meitei Organization
is impleaded as a party respondent.
5. The newly-impleaded respondent, instead of filing a counter-
affidavit,  shall  file  the  details  of  the  other  National
Highways/State Highways that are blocked, along with a proposal
regarding how all such highways can be made functional again. The
petitioner–organization will also submit a comprehensive proposal
in that regard.
6. Given  that  the  National  Highways  are  maintained  by  the
National Highways Authority of India, we deem it appropriate to
implead that Authority as a party respondent. Ordered accordingly.
7. Memo of parties be amended accordingly.
8. Issue notice, returnable on 28.09.2026.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. It is informed by the learned counsel for the State that after
registration of the subject FIR, physical possession of the land in
the dispute was handed over to respondent no.2 and she continues to
be in possession thereof.
2. It has also been pointed out that while the subject land is
situated in village Chakkbaghoniya, District Sagar, respondent no.2
resides in village Guda Amalada, District Sheopur. It appears to us
1

## Page 706

that respondent no.2, seemingly being an absentee landowner, may
find it difficult to protect her possession unless appropriate
directions are issued by this Court.
3. It is necessary to ascertain the viewpoint of respondent no.2,
who has not been served so far. 
4. The Secretary, District Legal Services Authority, Sheopur
(“DLSA”), is directed to visit the residence of respondent no.2 and
apprise  her  of  her  right  to  contest  these  proceedings.  The
Secretary, DLSA will also inform respondent no.2 that a sum of
Rs.25,000/- has been deposited with this Court towards litigation
expenses, which will be released to her once she enters appearance.
The  Secretary,  DLSA,  will  also  persuade  respondent  no.2  to
accompany them to the nearest jurisdictional court so that her
statement regarding the taking of physical possession and the
manner in which her possession can be duly protected in future may
be recorded. 
5. A  status  report  shall  thereafter  be  forwarded  by  the
Secretary, DLSA, through the State Legal Services Authority. The
Member Secretary, Madhya Pradesh State Legal Services Authority,
shall ensure compliance of this order.
6. Post the matter on 21.09.2026.
7. Interim order to continue.
